growth_story.headline: After cocoa shocks and civil war, income per person in Côte d'Ivoire has grown 4.1 percent a year since 2012, but is still below its 1978 peak.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in Côte d'Ivoire peaked in 1978, and in 2025 it was still 18.5 percent below that peak, about where it first was in 1971. From 1990 to 2003 it fell 2.1 percent a year: the sources trace this to falling cocoa prices and mounting debt, and then to a political crisis that brought a coup in 1999 and civil war in 2002; a rebound after the 1994 CFA franc devaluation (growth of 3.0 to 5.5 percent in 1995–1997) did not last. From 2004 to 2011 income per person was flat, at -0.1 percent a year, while the country stayed split in two until 2007, and the post-election conflict of 2010–2011 cut it by 7.4 percent in 2011. Since 2012 it has grown 4.1 percent a year, with 8.6 percent in 2013, as the end of the crisis, a surge in public investment and returning business and consumer confidence drove a rebound. Growth has stayed strong: 3.2 percent a year over 2016–2025 against 2.5 over 2006–2015, with one dip, -1.8 percent in 2020.

threads.title: Cocoa shocks and mounting debt
threads.text: From 1985, falling world cocoa prices hit an economy built on cocoa exports, and membership of the CFA franc zone ruled out a devaluation to soften the blow. Debt became unmanageable and public jobs and social services were cut, and income per person slid from its 1978 peak through the 1980s and into the 1990s.

since_last_year.text: Income per person grew 4.0 percent in 2025, close to the pace of the past decade, with strong investment and household spending behind it. In its October 2026 update the World Bank reports that public debt fell for the first time since 2012, and expects growth to slow slightly in 2026 as outside demand softens because of the Middle East conflict.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe a decade of fast total growth and one of Africa's most consistent performers. The data show smaller gains in income per person, 3.2 percent a year over 2016–2025, because a fast-growing population takes a large share of total growth. And after 14 years of recovery, income per person in 2025 was still 18.5 percent below its 1978 peak, about where it first was in 1971.
